narration.say: On November 18th, Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth.
So how do we still hear its fridge-bulb radio?
cues: So how do we still hear

narration.say: Radio spreads out like light: twice as far, a quarter of the power.
By Earth, less than a billion-billionth of a watt arrives.
Its dish narrows the beam, and 70-meter dishes catch it.
The catch: its nuclear power drops about 4 watts every year.
Out there, bigger ears beat a louder voice.
Follow Media Diet for the physics behind the headlines.

shots.beat: first frame / hook: paper Voyager 1 with a golden radio ring arriving from tiny Earth + "24 hours / to say hello."
one light-day: a pulse leaves Earth and needs one full sweep of a 24-hour dial to reach Voyager; NASA date chip
the question: over Voyager's shoulder toward a tiny Earth; a fridge bulb for the radio's scale
inverse square: same light over one tile at distance 1, four tiles at distance 2
at Earth: a beam footprint far wider than the planet, a few faint sparks
Voyager's dish squeezes the radio into a narrow cone
a 70-meter Deep Space Network dish catches the sparks (person for scale)
the constraint: the nuclear power source glows; a power gauge drops
takeaway: a big dish beside a small one — the big one catches far more
CTA: Media Diet sign, a small paper Voyager on a stick behind it
